Bias-Only Training Dynamics in ReLU Networks

Shreyas Chaudhari    José M. F. Moura
Abstract

Neural networks with randomly initialized, fixed weights and trainable biases are universal approximators, yet the dynamics of bias-only training remain largely unexplored. We study these dynamics in one-hidden-layer ReLU networks through activation codes, the binary patterns of active neurons that partition the input space into convex polyhedral regions. We show that the gradients with respect to the biases depend on each input only through its activation code, and hence the training dynamics can be characterized with these codes. In particular, as long as the activation codes remain fixed, training reduces to a linear least-squares problem with the codes as features. Training can then be understood as a sequence of least-squares problems, with transitions occurring when neurons change their activation states. We show that the fraction of switching neurons vanishes as the network widens, and the training dynamics approach those of linear least squares on the initial activation codes in the infinite-width limit. Our experiments support these theoretical findings, showing that while activation switches can noticeably affect training in narrower networks, their relative frequency and the associated changes in the dynamics diminish as the width increases.

Index Terms: 
Deep learning, training dynamics, ReLU, Hamming, kernels
††address: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Carnegie Mellon University

1 Introduction

Characterizing the training dynamics of neural networks is a central step toward explaining how they transform data into useful representations. In wide networks, these dynamics are described by the neural tangent kernel (NTK) [19], under which learning reduces to kernel regression [21, 2, 8]. These results concern training all weights and biases, yet recent work shows that the biases alone carry substantial expressive power. Neural networks with random, frozen weights and learned biases are universal approximators [28], and bias-only fine-tuning is competitive for adapting large models [5]. The dynamics of bias-only training, however, remain largely unexplored.

We study bias-only training of ReLU networks and show that its dynamics are governed by the inherently combinatorial structure of these networks. A ReLU network is a continuous piecewise affine function that partitions its input space into convex polyhedra, each indexed by an activation code, the binary vector of neurons active at an input. The number of codes is related to expressivity [23, 18], and their distribution under random inputs determines the distribution of the affine functions a trained network realizes [7]. We show that these codes also govern training: the gradient of the network output with respect to the biases is a signed, scaled copy of the activation code, so each input affects training only through its code. Consequently, the NTK is exactly a kernel on activation codes, and two inputs are treated similarly to the extent that their codes agree.

Contributions. We show that for ReLU networks trained only through their biases, the NTK is exactly a linear kernel on activation codes at any width and throughout training, and that it changes only when neurons flip (Proposition 1). Without flips, training is exactly least squares on the codes, and it can fit arbitrary training targets if and only if the code matrix has full row rank (Proposition 2). The squared distance that the NTK induces between inputs is proportional to the Hamming distance between their codes, which bounds how differently two inputs evolve during training (Proposition 3). At initialization, the codes are random-hyperplane hashes, and the kernel converges to a scaled collision probability, namely the arc-cosine kernel [10] (Proposition 4). Finally, we show that at most O⁡(m)O(\sqrt{m}) neurons flip per input, yet their fraction and the resulting kernel drift both shrink as O(m−1/2)O(m^{-1/2}) (Proposition 5), as confirmed by simulations.

Related work. Bounding the number of ReLU units that change state during training is central to over-parameterized convergence proofs [12, 3, 1, 24], while finite-width NTK corrections [17], activation flips under large bias initialization [29], and hidden-feature drift under lazy training [27] have been studied. The expressivity and practical benefits of bias-only and other partial training have been studied [28, 5, 14], but the training dynamics of such settings have received comparatively little attention. Training only the output layer of a random network yields a random-feature model [26]; bias-only training instead moves the hidden features themselves. The geometry of ReLU networks has been studied through their number of regions, polyhedral structure, and distribution [23, 4, 15, 7], as well as through kernels defined by gating patterns and neural paths [13, 20]. Hamming distances between random-hyperplane codes approximate angles [16, 6], and random (biased) tessellations preserve and separate data [25, 11]. In this paper, we connect the geometry of activation codes in ReLU networks directly to the bias-only training regime.

2.2 ReLU Networks and Activation Codes

Let f:ℝd→ℝf:{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\to{\mathbb{R}} be a one-hidden-layer network with mm units, weight scale sw>0s_{w}>0, and bias scale sb>0s_{b}>0,

𝐡⁡(𝐱)\displaystyle{\mathbf{h}}({\mathbf{x}}) =swd​𝐖1​𝐱+sb​𝐛,f⁡(𝐱)=swm​𝐰2⊤​σ​(𝐡⁡(𝐱))\displaystyle=\frac{s_{w}}{\sqrt{d}}\,{\mathbf{W}}_{1}{\mathbf{x}}+s_{b}\,{\mathbf{b}},\;\qquad f({\mathbf{x}})=\frac{s_{w}}{\sqrt{m}}\,{\mathbf{w}}_{2}^{\top}\sigma\left({\mathbf{h}}({\mathbf{x}})\right) (7)

The entries of 𝐖1{\mathbf{W}}_{1}, whose jjth row we denote 𝐰1,j⊤{\mathbf{w}}_{1,j}^{\top}, and of 𝐛{\mathbf{b}} are initialized i.i.d. 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1), and those of 𝐰2{\mathbf{w}}_{2} are i.i.d. uniform on {±1}\{\pm 1\}. We train only the bias 𝐛{\mathbf{b}}, keeping the weights fixed at their random initial values. This parameterization is consistent with the standard infinite-width scaling under which the NTK admits a well-defined limit as m→∞m\to\infty [19, 21].

The activation code is defined as

𝐳(𝐱)=𝟙[𝐡(𝐱)>0]∈{0,1}m\displaystyle{\mathbf{z}}({\mathbf{x}})=\mathbbm{1}\left[{\mathbf{h}}({\mathbf{x}})>0\right]\in\{0,1\}^{m} (8)

ReLU networks are continuous piecewise affine functions over convex polyhedral partitions of the input space. Two inputs with the same full activation code belong to the same linear region. For two inputs 𝐱,𝐱′{\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}, the Hamming distance (number of bit differences) between their activation codes is

dH​(𝐱,𝐱′)=#⁡{j:zj​(𝐱)≠zj​(𝐱′)}=‖𝐳⁡(𝐱)−𝐳⁡(𝐱′)‖22.\displaystyle d_{H}({\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime})=\#\{j:z_{j}({\mathbf{x}})\neq z_{j}({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime})\}=\|{\mathbf{z}}({\mathbf{x}})-{\mathbf{z}}({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime})\|_{2}^{2}. (9)

3 Bias-Only Training Dynamics

We study the training dynamics when only the bias 𝐛{\mathbf{b}} is learned by gradient flow. Throughout, we use the notation 𝐫t=ft​(𝐗)−𝐲\mathbf{r}_{t}=f_{t}({\mathbf{X}})-{\mathbf{y}} for the training residual at time tt, c=sb2​sw2c=s_{b}^{2}s_{w}^{2}, and 𝐃⁡(𝐱)=diag⁡(𝐳⁡(𝐱)){\mathbf{D}}({\mathbf{x}})=\mathrm{diag}({\mathbf{z}}({\mathbf{x}})). The gradient of the network output with respect to the bias is

∇𝐛f​(𝐱)=cm​𝐰2⊙𝐳⁡(𝐱).\displaystyle\nabla_{\mathbf{b}}f({\mathbf{x}})=\sqrt{\tfrac{c}{m}}\,{\mathbf{w}}_{2}\odot{\mathbf{z}}({\mathbf{x}}). (10)

The gradient therefore depends on the input only through its activation code and is piecewise constant with respect to the inputs.

These thresholds partition each coordinate of the bias vector into intervals with fixed activation states, and together they form an axis-aligned grid in bias space. Within each cell kk, the training codes 𝐙k\mathbf{Z}_{k} remain fixed, and so does 𝜼k\boldsymbol{\eta}_{k}, the vector of values η⁡(𝐱i)\eta({\mathbf{x}}_{i}). When an entry of the bias crosses a threshold, the corresponding activation bit flips, so the dynamics switch to those of the neighboring cell. Bias-only training thus proceeds through a sequence of least-squares problems, and Proposition 2 describes the special case in which no threshold is crossed.

3.2 Linear Code Kernel Induces Hamming Geometry

Recall that the Hamming distance (9) counts the neuron hyperplanes separating two inputs (Figure 1). By (10), and since w2,j2=1w_{2,j}^{2}=1,

‖∇𝐛f​(𝐱)−∇𝐛f​(𝐱′)‖22=cm​dH​(𝐱,𝐱′).\displaystyle\|\nabla_{\mathbf{b}}f({\mathbf{x}})-\nabla_{\mathbf{b}}f({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime})\|_{2}^{2}=\tfrac{c}{m}d_{H}({\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}). (11)

The Hamming distance hence measures how differently two inputs respond to bias updates. Expanding (9) with Proposition 1(i) also gives

Θ⁡(𝐱,𝐱′)=c2​m​(‖𝐳⁡(𝐱)‖22+‖𝐳⁡(𝐱′)‖22−dH​(𝐱,𝐱′)),\displaystyle\Theta({\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime})=\tfrac{c}{2m}\big(\|{\mathbf{z}}({\mathbf{x}})\|_{2}^{2}+\|{\mathbf{z}}({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime})\|_{2}^{2}-d_{H}({\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime})\big), (12)

so the kernel decreases with Hamming distance, offset by the number of neurons active at each input. The following proposition relates this geometry to the training dynamics.

Proposition 3 (Hamming-close inputs train alike).

Let the Hamming distance at time tt be dH,t​(𝐱,𝐱′)=‖𝐳t​(𝐱)−𝐳t​(𝐱′)‖22d_{H,t}({\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime})=\|{\mathbf{z}}_{t}({\mathbf{x}})-{\mathbf{z}}_{t}({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime})\|_{2}^{2}. Under gradient flow, for almost every tt,

|dd​t​[ft​(𝐱)−ft​(𝐱′)]|≤cm​dH,t​(𝐱,𝐱′)​‖𝐫t‖1.\left|\tfrac{d}{dt}[f_{t}({\mathbf{x}})-f_{t}({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime})]\right|\leq\tfrac{c}{m}d_{H,t}({\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime})\,\|\mathbf{r}_{t}\|_{1}.

By the NTK dynamics,

dd​t[ft(𝐱)−ft(𝐱′)]=−∑i=1n[Θt(𝐱,𝐱i)−Θt(𝐱′,𝐱i)]rt,i.\tfrac{d}{dt}[f_{t}({\mathbf{x}})-f_{t}({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime})]=-\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\Theta_{t}({\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{x}}_{i})-\Theta_{t}({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime},{\mathbf{x}}_{i})]\,r_{t,i}.

By Proposition 1(i), each kernel difference is cm​∑j(zt,j​(𝐱)−zt,j​(𝐱′))​zt,j​(𝐱i)\tfrac{c}{m}\sum_{j}\big(z_{t,j}({\mathbf{x}})-z_{t,j}({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime})\big)z_{t,j}({\mathbf{x}}_{i}). Since zt,j​(𝐱i)∈{0,1}z_{t,j}({\mathbf{x}}_{i})\in\{0,1\}, each term is at most |zt,j​(𝐱)−zt,j​(𝐱′)||z_{t,j}({\mathbf{x}})-z_{t,j}({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime})| in magnitude, which equals 11 if the two inputs differ in bit jj and 00 otherwise. Hence |Θt​(𝐱,𝐱i)−Θt​(𝐱′,𝐱i)|≤cm​dH,t​(𝐱,𝐱′)|\Theta_{t}({\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{x}}_{i})-\Theta_{t}({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime},{\mathbf{x}}_{i})|\leq\tfrac{c}{m}d_{H,t}({\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}). Applying the triangle inequality to the sum and this bound to each term gives the result, since ∑i|rt,i|=‖𝐫t‖1\sum_{i}|r_{t,i}|=\|\mathbf{r}_{t}\|_{1}. ∎

Thus inputs with similar codes receive similar updates, and inputs with identical codes receive the same updates, so their prediction difference stays constant while their codes coincide, however far apart they are in input space.

3.3 Infinite Width: Random Hyperplane Codes

The preceding results hold for arbitrary biases and arbitrary network widths. We now consider the infinite-width limit (m→∞)(m\to\infty) at initialization. Let 𝐠j=(𝐰1,j,bj)∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈d+1)\mathbf{g}_{j}=({\mathbf{w}}_{1,j},b_{j})\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}_{d+1}) and 𝐱¯=(sw​𝐱/d,sb)\bar{\mathbf{x}}=(s_{w}{\mathbf{x}}/\sqrt{d},s_{b}), so that hj​(𝐱)=𝐠j⊤​𝐱¯h_{j}({\mathbf{x}})=\mathbf{g}_{j}^{\top}\bar{\mathbf{x}}. Additionally, we denote by ϕ\phi the angle between 𝐱¯\bar{\mathbf{x}} and 𝐱¯′\bar{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}.

Proposition 4 (Random hyperplane codes).

Let Θ⋆​(𝐱,𝐱′)=c2​(1−ϕ/π)\Theta^{\star}({\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime})=\tfrac{c}{2}(1-\phi/\pi). At initialization, for any fixed 𝐱,𝐱′{\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}:

  1. (i)

    𝔼⁡[dH​(𝐱,𝐱′)]/m=ϕ/π\mathbb{E}[d_{H}({\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime})]/m=\phi/\pi;

  2. (ii)

    𝔼⁡[Θ0​(𝐱,𝐱′)]=Θ⋆​(𝐱,𝐱′)\mathbb{E}[\Theta_{0}({\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime})]=\Theta^{\star}({\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime});

  3. (iii)

    with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, |Θ0​(𝐱,𝐱′)−Θ⋆​(𝐱,𝐱′)|≤c​log⁡(2/δ)/(2​m)|\Theta_{0}({\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime})-\Theta^{\star}({\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime})|\leq c\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/(2m)}.

Proof.

Each neuron defines a random hyperplane separating 𝐱¯\bar{\mathbf{x}} and 𝐱¯′\bar{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime} with probability ϕ/π\phi/\pi [16, 6], giving (i). By symmetry, both inputs are active with probability (1−ϕ/π)/2(1-\phi/\pi)/2, a Gaussian orthant probability [7]. Taking expectations in Θ0​(𝐱,𝐱′)=cm​∑jzj​(𝐱)​zj​(𝐱′)\Theta_{0}({\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime})=\tfrac{c}{m}\sum_{j}z_{j}({\mathbf{x}})z_{j}({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}) gives (ii). Since the summands are independent and bounded, Hoeffding’s inequality gives Pr(|Θ0−Θ⋆|≥ε)≤2e−2mε2/c2\Pr(|\Theta_{0}-\Theta^{\star}|\geq\varepsilon)\leq 2e^{-2m\varepsilon^{2}/c^{2}}, which implies (iii). ∎

At initialization, the angle between lifted inputs thus sets the expected Hamming distance between their codes. Inputs at a small angle share most bits and train alike, while inputs at a large angle are weakly coupled. As the width grows, the kernel concentrates around Θ⋆\Theta^{\star}, a scaled degree-zero arc-cosine kernel on the lifted inputs [10].

3.4 How Wide Is Wide Enough?

By Proposition 1(ii), the kernel changes only when activation codes change. Increasing width does not eliminate code flips but reduces their fraction.

Proposition 5 (Code flips diminish with width).

Suppose ‖𝐱i‖2=1\|{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\|_{2}=1 for all training inputs, and fix a training horizon TT and δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1). There exists a constant KK, independent of mm, such that with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T] and all i,ji,j,

τt​(𝐱i)≤K​m,|Θt​(𝐱i,𝐱j)−Θ0​(𝐱i,𝐱j)|≤2​c​Km.\tau_{t}({\mathbf{x}}_{i})\leq K\sqrt{m},\qquad|\Theta_{t}({\mathbf{x}}_{i},{\mathbf{x}}_{j})-\Theta_{0}({\mathbf{x}}_{i},{\mathbf{x}}_{j})|\leq\frac{2cK}{\sqrt{m}}.
Proof.

Following [12, 29], we bound the bias movement, code flips, and kernel drift.

Bias movement. Gradient flow does not increase the loss, so ‖𝐫t‖2≤‖𝐫0‖2\|\mathbf{r}_{t}\|_{2}\leq\|\mathbf{r}_{0}\|_{2}. At initialization, 𝔼⁡[f0​(𝐱i)2]=sw2​q/2\mathbb{E}[f_{0}({\mathbf{x}}_{i})^{2}]=s_{w}^{2}q/2, where q=‖𝐱¯i‖22=sw2/d+sb2q=\|\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\|_{2}^{2}=s_{w}^{2}/d+s_{b}^{2}, so 𝔼​‖𝐫0‖22\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{r}_{0}\|_{2}^{2} is independent of mm. By Markov’s inequality, there exists BB, independent of mm, such that ‖𝐫0‖2≤B\|\mathbf{r}_{0}\|_{2}\leq B with probability at least 1−δ/21-\delta/2. On this event, (10) gives

|b˙t,j|≤c/m​‖𝐫t‖1≤B​c​n/m.|\dot{b}_{t,j}|\leq\sqrt{c/m}\,\|\mathbf{r}_{t}\|_{1}\leq B\sqrt{cn/m}.

Each bias therefore moves by at most R=T​B​c​n/mR=TB\sqrt{cn/m} over [0,T][0,T].

Code flips. A neuron can change state at 𝐱i{\mathbf{x}}_{i} only if |h0,j​(𝐱i)|≤sb​R|h_{0,j}({\mathbf{x}}_{i})|\leq s_{b}R. Since h0,j​(𝐱i)∼𝒩⁡(0,q)h_{0,j}({\mathbf{x}}_{i})\sim\mathcal{N}(0,q) with q≥sb2q\geq s_{b}^{2}, this event has probability at most 2/πR=O(m−1/2)\sqrt{2/\pi}R=O(m^{-1/2}). Hence the expected number of neurons close enough to flip at each input is O⁡(m)O(\sqrt{m}). Markov’s inequality and a union bound over the nn training inputs imply that, with probability at least 1−δ/21-\delta/2, this number is at most K​mK\sqrt{m} for every input, for a suitable constant KK independent of mm. Consequently, τt​(𝐱i)≤K​m\tau_{t}({\mathbf{x}}_{i})\leq K\sqrt{m} for all t≤Tt\leq T.

Kernel drift. By Proposition 1(ii),

|Θt​(𝐱i,𝐱j)−Θ0​(𝐱i,𝐱j)|≤cm​(τt​(𝐱i)+τt​(𝐱j))≤2​c​K/m.|\Theta_{t}({\mathbf{x}}_{i},{\mathbf{x}}_{j})-\Theta_{0}({\mathbf{x}}_{i},{\mathbf{x}}_{j})|\leq\tfrac{c}{m}(\tau_{t}({\mathbf{x}}_{i})+\tau_{t}({\mathbf{x}}_{j}))\leq 2cK/\sqrt{m}.

A union bound completes the proof. ∎

Although the number of code flips may grow with width, their fraction and the kernel drift vanish as O(m−1/2)O(m^{-1/2}) with high probability. With Proposition 4, the kernel thus approaches Θ⋆\Theta^{\star} over any fixed horizon, recovering the lazy-training regime.

4 Experiments

We train the biases of a one-hidden-layer network with sw2=2s_{w}^{2}=2 and sb=1s_{b}=1 (so c=2c=2), initialized as in Section 2, using full-batch gradient descent with step size 1/λmax​(𝚯0)1/\lambda_{\max}({\boldsymbol{\Theta}}_{0}). The n=30n=30 training inputs and 500500 test inputs are drawn uniformly from the unit sphere in ℝ5{\mathbb{R}}^{5}, with targets y=sin⁡(2​x1)+12​x22y=\sin(2x_{1})+\frac{1}{2}x_{2}^{2}. To study nearby inputs, we create a perturbed version of each of 100100 test inputs at a distance between 10−310^{-3} and 10−110^{-1}. We train for 30003000 steps with network widths m∈{256,1024,4096,16384}m\in\{256,1024,4096,16384\}.

Figure 2(a) plots the initial kernel against the Hamming distance between test inputs. By (12),

Θ0c=12​(1−dHm)+‖𝐳0​(𝐱)‖22+‖𝐳0​(𝐱′)‖22−m2​m,\frac{\Theta_{0}}{c}=\frac{1}{2}\Big(1-\frac{d_{H}}{m}\Big)+\frac{\|{\mathbf{z}}_{0}({\mathbf{x}})\|_{2}^{2}+\|{\mathbf{z}}_{0}({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime})\|_{2}^{2}-m}{2m},

where ‖𝐳0​(𝐱)‖22\|{\mathbf{z}}_{0}({\mathbf{x}})\|_{2}^{2} counts the neurons active at 𝐱{\mathbf{x}}. The second term has mean zero and is of order m−1/2m^{-1/2}. At m=256m=256, only 43%43\% of the biases are positive, so most points lie slightly below 12​(1−dH/m)\frac{1}{2}(1-d_{H}/m). As width increases, the points concentrate around this line, as predicted by Proposition 4.

Figure 2(b) tests Proposition 3 using all pairs among the 100100 selected test inputs and their nearby copies. For each pair, the vertical axis shows the change in prediction difference over training, namely |[fT​(𝐱)−fT​(𝐱′)]−[f0​(𝐱)−f0​(𝐱′)]||[f_{T}({\mathbf{x}})-f_{T}({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime})]-[f_{0}({\mathbf{x}})-f_{0}({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime})]|, while the horizontal axis shows the bound from Proposition 3, summed over training steps and multiplied by the step size. We observe that nearby input pairs (crosses) have similar activation codes and small changes in prediction difference, with all observed changes below the bound (dashed diagonal).

Figure 2(c) and the first three columns of Table 1 test Proposition 5. As the width increases from m=256m=256 to m=16384m=16384, the number τT\tau_{T} of flipped bits per training input rises from 3232 to 231231, while the fraction τT/m\tau_{T}/m decreases from 0.1250.125 to 0.0140.014 (blue circles). The fitted exponents, +0.48+0.48 and −0.52-0.52, are consistent with the O⁡(m)O(\sqrt{m}) and O(m−1/2)O(m^{-1/2}) bounds of Proposition 5. The fraction of flipped bits at test inputs (green squares) closely matches that at training inputs. Each flip changes a kernel entry by at most c/mc/m, so the decreasing fraction of flipped bits keeps the kernel drift small.

The kernel drift decreases from 0.0650.065 to 0.00280.0028 as the width increases (Figure 2(d)), with a fitted slope of −0.75-0.75, faster than the m−1/2m^{-1/2} bound of Proposition 5. The bound accounts for every flip, although a flip at 𝐱{\mathbf{x}} affects Θ⁡(𝐱,𝐱′)\Theta({\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}) only when the neuron is also active at 𝐱′{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}, and flips in opposite directions can cancel. As the width increases, the trained network also approaches the fixed-code predictor of Proposition 2, which keeps all activation codes at their initial values. The difference between their test predictions, relative to the change in the fixed-code predictor from initialization, decreases from 17%17\% to 1.5%1.5\%, while the training loss falls from 10−2.210^{-2.2} to 10−7.510^{-7.5} (Table 1). Thus, even though activation codes continue to change, the training dynamics of wide networks are well described by least squares on their initial codes.

5 Conclusion

We have shown that when only the biases of a ReLU network are trained, the training dynamics are governed by its binary activation codes. The NTK is a linear kernel on these codes at any width, and inputs with similar codes undergo similar changes in their predictions. Between changes in activation states, training is linear least squares on the codes. As the network width increases, the number of activation switches per input grows at most as O⁡(m)O(\sqrt{m}), while their fraction vanishes. As a result, the kernel drift decreases as O(m−1/2)O(m^{-1/2}), and the kernel approaches its infinite-width limit. Together, these results connect the discrete structure of the regions formed by ReLU activations with the continuous dynamics of training. Future work may study extensions to deeper networks.
